newsitem.title: INDIA: India, Pakistan to resume long-stalled dialogue.
newsitem.headline: India, Pakistan to resume long-stalled dialogue.

text.p: Arch-rivals Pakistan and India prepared on Friday to resume a dialogue that collapsed in January 1994 over the disputed Himalayan territory of Kashmir.
For Pakistan, Kashmir remains the "core issue", but India is hoping for progress on trade and economic cooperation as a means of easing tension between South Asia's threshold nuclear powers.

"Our focus is on cooperation," Indian Foreign Minister Inder Kumar Gujral said in an interview published in the April issue of the English-language magazine Frontline. "My position on this is very simple: let them trade with us if it suits them."

He said India wanted good neighbourly ties with Pakistan based on the 1972 Shimla Agreement between the two countries, but would not renounce "sovereignty" over Kashmir, even though it was prepared to discuss the dispute.

"Naturally, Indian sovereignty is not negotiable," he declared. "Unless both of us understand this, difficulties will continue. We have given them (Pakistan) several concessions, like travel, unilaterally. We plan to expand these further."
India last week eased visa restrictions on Pakistanis after Islamabad released 38 Indian children held along with scores of adult Indian fishermen caught in Pakistani territorial waters.
Shamshad Ahmad, Pakistan's foreign secretary leading a six-man team, called on Gujral on Friday morning. "It went off very well. It was just a courtesy call," Ahmad told reporters afterwards.
Underlining the caution on both sides, Ahmad said when asked if there would be any public statements: "We are not going to talk about the talks. It has been agreed upon."
Formal talks between Ahmad and his Indian opposite number Salman Haider were scheduled to start at 3.30 p.m. (1000 GMT).
If the talks between the two countries' top diplomats go well, the Indian and Pakistani foreign ministers will meet after an April 7-8 Non-Aligned Movement conference in New Delhi.

That could pave the way for discussions between Indian Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda and his Pakistani counterpart Nawaz Sharif at a summit of the South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation (SAARC) in the Maldives from May 12 to 14.
Witnesses said Kashmiri separatists gathered near Hyderabad House, venue of the four-day talks, to protest at the exclusion of the umbrella All Parties Hurriyat (Freedom) Conference.

The Hurriyat bands some 30 religious and political groups demanding a plebiscite in Kashmir that Pakistan, citing U.N. resolutions, has been campaigning for. India wants the dispute to be resolved bilaterally under the Shimla accord.
Pakistan's Foreign Minister Gohar Ayub told parliament in Islamabad on Thursday there could be no normalisation of the situation in South Asia without a solution for Kashmir.

"He declared that Pakistan, as in the past, would continue its moral, political and diplomatic support for Kashmiris in their struggle for their right of self-determination in line with U.N. resolutions," state-run Pakistan radio said.
Tension between India and Pakistan worsened after Kashmiris began a revolt against Indian rule in 1990 in the two-thirds of the territory held by New Delhi. Pakistan controls the rest.
India and Pakistan have gone to war three times since independence from Britain in 1947, twice over Kashmir.

In his interview with Frontline, Gujral suggested that India's approach to its border dispute with China, involving talks, confidence-building measures and cooperation in other areas, could be a model for reducing conflict with Pakistan.
"I had personally suggested that we put the issue of Kashmir on the back-burner," he said. "We did not mean that they should forget about it."
